extraction.name: Common Corpus
extraction.description: The largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing about two trillion tokens from uncopyrighted or permissively licensed multilingual text and code sources.
extraction.creator: PleIAs, Paris, France
extraction.inLanguage: en, fr, de, zh, it, es, ja, pl, la, nl, ru, ar, ko
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. Data were collected from public domain and permissively licensed sources using APIs, standard retrieval methods, direct extractions, and reuse of existing open datasets, with provenance and license verification documented.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Software Collection, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include Collections As Data dumps, Internet Archive, Delpher, OpenAlex, arXiv, Stack v1 and v2, Wikimedia projects, YouTube transcripts, StackExchange, and Wikidata, as well as government, legal, financial, and cultural heritage repositories.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For Wikidata, items and properties were converted into formal natural language sequences, and all available translations were provided as consecutive blocks separated by a newline.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing and curation included text segmentation, OCR quality detection, OCR correction, PII removal, toxicity filtering, license filtering, file-type filtering, and manual quality filters. For code, files outside desired languages and formats were removed, licenses were filtered to permissible ones, low-quality files were discarded, digit-heavy files were removed, and line breaks were normalized.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, was trained from scratch on 2M annotated samples to identify toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Microsoft Presidio, Celadon, fastText language identification model, cld2
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource, with past versions archived on Hugging Face for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally identifiable information (PII), including phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses, was addressed and removed or replaced.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support open science LLM research and development while meeting legal and regulatory requirements, and to serve as shared infrastructure for different communities.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that historical public domain texts may contain harmful language and outdated norms regarding ethnic groups, women, violence, and other themes, which could lead models to reproduce harmful language. The toxicity filtering pipeline aims to mitigate these biases and harms.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset does not cover all available open data, has shallow coverage for low-resource languages, is suitable mainly for pre-training models of limited size, does not contain instruction-tuning or specialized task data, and curation methods do not achieve 100% accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primarily for language model pre-training; can also be used to create multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, benchmarks, vision-language models for document processing, historical language models, creative writing models, and retrieval-augmented generation resources. It is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training.

description.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training. The data assembled in Common Corpus are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses and amount to about two trillion tokens.

publisher.evidence: Common Corpus is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files

datePublished.evidence: The current version of Common Corpus, the one we describe in this paper, was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.

isLiveDataset.evidence: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring a proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Common Corpus is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files and is composed of six collections: Open Govemment, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. All other parts of Open Culture have been collected on a resource-by-resource basis using APIs and other standard retrieval methods whenever available.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: All other parts of Open Culture have been collected on a resource-by-resource basis using APIs and other standard retrieval methods whenever available. OpenAlex maintains an expansive API search engine tracking detailed metadata for each indexed item, including the licensing, as well as a link to the original resource, which is generally in PDF format. The code data we use comes from the Stack v1 and v2. A large part of Open Culture is compiled from Collections As Data (CAD) — large dumps of texts, datasets, PDFs, and even raw XML output (METS/ALTO).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: A large part of Open Culture is compiled from Collections As Data (CAD) — large dumps of texts, datasets, PDFs, and even raw XML output (METS/ALTO). OpenAlex maintains an expansive API search engine tracking detailed metadata for each indexed item, including the licensing, as well as a link to the original resource, which is generally in PDF format. The code data we use comes from the Stack v1 and v2. Wikipedia and Wikisource. Wikimedia projects have always been major sources for language model training due to their reliability, extensive coverage, and textbook-like style. Youtube Commons. YouTube Commons is our collection of audio transcripts of 2,063,066 videos uploaded on YouTube under a standardized CC-By license. Semantic data is the latest set added to Common Corpus and currently includes only one collection: Wikidata.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: In this paper, we present Common Corpus , which has been an ongoing effort since 2024 (see Appendix A for the development history). The current version of Common Corpus, the one we describe in this paper, was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: Data processing involved the translation of items and properties into formal language sequences as simple natural language sequences, without textual synthesis: “Q41309 | P:27 | Q171150” becoming “Franz Liszt country of citizenship Kingdom of Hungary”. Within each entry, we provide all the available translations as consecutive blocks separated by a newline, anticipating that this may contribute to language alignment.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Here, we detail the composition of Common Corpus (Section 3), as well as the data provenance, license verification, and further processing (Section 4). To prepare the collection, we ran a pipeline of varied filters. We first removed files that were not in our desired set of languages and formats according to their file extensions... We then filtered out the licenses to keep only permissible ones. To discard the low-quality data, we ran a series of manual filters described by Lozhkov et al. (2024). In addition to those, we removed files consisting of 75% or more of digits, which are mostly files containing raw numeric data. Before the filters, we also replaced sequences of [\r]+\n with \n and recalculated line lengths to avoid false positives by maximum line length.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We created a multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, a DeBERTa-v3-small model ( ∼140M parameters), which we trained from scratch on 2M annotated samples. Celadon identifies toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: For text segmentation, we developed Segmentext. We developed two pipelines to determine the digitization quality of different datasets... OCRoscope. OCRerrcr. We developed OCRonos model based on Llama 3 8B. To identify and replace PII, we use Microsoft’s Presidio, an open-source state-of-the-art tool. We created a multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon. Language distribution was computed using the fastText language identification model. This is a tool based on the language identification tool cld2.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring a proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: Do not capture highly sensitive data. We remove personally identifiable information from our datasets (Section 4.4). In an analysis of large open datasets, there is a staggering amount of personal data in widely used datasets, e.g., large quantities of phone numbers in RedPajama, email addresses in S2ORC and peS2o, and IP addresses in the Stack (Elazar et al., 2024).

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Through the release of this dataset, we show that open LLM research and development is possible while meeting legal and regulatory requirements—even in the EU, where AI regulations are currently the strictest. As defined by UNESCO, it is a shared research infrastructure that is needed to support open science and serve the needs of different communities (Unesco, 2021).

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Many texts there are historical periodicals and monographs from at least 80 years ago. Cultural norms surrounding the discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence have changed dramatically. Many of these texts, therefore, do not meet modem ethical standards. Training models on these texts would lead to the reproduction and circulation of harmful language. With this approach, we aim to mitigate some of the potential biases and harms in the dataset, while still leveraging the high-quality and stylistically diverse data for high model performance.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Common Corpus is far from collecting the whole range of available open data, which we call the open data paradox. In addition to this, even though the language diversity of the data is large, the coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. Furthermore, the amount of collected data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training of models of limited size... In addition, Common Corpus naturally does not contain data for instruction-tuning and any forms of specialized tasks. Therefore, it is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. Even though we used these methods responsibly and mitigated many issues overlooked by the counterparts... none of the curation methods could naturally facilitate a hundred-percent accuracy.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training. One application for this dataset is to develop vision-language models (VLMs) for advanced document segmentation and processing. Therefore, Open Culture contributes data that can be used to train models for creative writing without violating copyright law. As many of the Open Culture datasets are historical... this collection also enables the development of historical language models. It has been used to create a wider range of language model artifacts, including multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks. Therefore, it is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning.
